summary: Round-2 test pass over the gate and its six fixtures. The round-1 defect is dead: reverting the predicate to substring-in-an-eight-line-window is now killed by three of the six rows (unmetered, metered-on-one-branch-only, commented-out), and I reproduced the author's probe over the real 700-line store -- not only deletion of each of the twelve record("...") lines (12/12) but also commenting each out (12/12), renaming each to recordLater( (12/12) and moving each below an inserted early return (12/12). The evidence is sound for the four ways a verb goes unmetered in place. What it does not cover is a gate that never LOOKS at the verb, and that is the one finding: I mutated the script so that only the first @Override in the file is examined, and so that verbs past line 100 are skipped -- both leave all six fixture rows AND both @Test cases green, because every fixture is under 26 lines and every fixture's unmetered verb is the FIRST one (round 1's fix moved it there, and moving it created the symmetric blind spot). Doubling the reported verb count and repointing the default TARGET at metered.java survive for the same reason: nothing in the suite asserts WHICH file the gate examined or HOW MANY verbs it found. One fixture with an unmetered verb BETWEEN two metered ones, plus two contains(...) substrings on the real-store case, closes all four -- this is a one-fixture gap in a fixture-shaped deliverable, not a sign the commit is too big. Two minors, both with surviving mutations named. Noted and NOT raised: far-away.java and metered-on-one-branch-only.java are the same input to the current predicate (both report `first statement is: if (k == null) {` at line 12) so neither kills a mutation the other misses today -- far-away earns its place as a regression fixture against round 1's window, and commented-out earns its place by killing a two-line lookahead loosening, which I measured.

findings.finding: The suite constrains the gate's VERDICT but never its SCOPE. Four mutations of scripts/check-fault-store-records.sh leave all six CsvSource rows and both @Test cases green, measured by running each mutant over all eight inputs: (1) examine only the first @Override in the file (`overrides=[k for k,l in enumerate(src) if '@Override' in l and not is_comment(l)]` + `if i != overrides[0]: continue`); (2) `if '@Override' not in line or is_comment(line) or i > 100:` -- every verb past line 100 of a 700-line file goes unexamined; (3) `COUNT=$(( $(grep -c ...) * 2 ))` -- the ok line overstates what was examined; (4) `TARGET="${1:-buildSrc/src/test/resources/fault-store-fixtures/metered.java}"` -- the default target, which is the ONLY target the pre-commit hook ever uses (pass_filenames: false), no longer names the fault-injecting store. (1) and (2) survive because every fixture is under 26 lines and every fixture's unmetered verb is FIRST -- round 1 moved it there to kill the forward-bleeding window, and that move left the backward direction unrepresented. (3) and (4) survive because line 106 asserts only `contains("verb(s) metered")`, while the ok line already prints both the count and the path.
findings.failure_scenario: FaultInjectingStore.java is at exactly 700 lines, on check-file-size's ceiling, so its next change is a split -- the gate's own header says so and no-verbs.java exists for it. A split that leaves six verbs in the file and moves six to a sibling produces `ok 6 verb(s) metered`, green, with half the verbs unguarded; the no-verbs fixture only catches the all-or-nothing version of that. Equally, a later edit that bounds or short-circuits the scan loop reports `ok 12 verb(s) metered` while having examined one verb. Both are the round-1 defect class exactly -- the predicate silently covering the wrong extent -- and the only thing that caught the round-1 instance was a manual probe over the real file, which is not in the tree and will not be re-run when the script next changes. The next unmetered verb then reaches a release path and reds a floor with no defect present, which is the M5.29 history this whole task exists to end.
findings.suggestion: One fixture and two substrings. Add `unmetered-in-the-middle.java` with three verbs -- metered, unmetered, metered -- and a row `| 1 | not metered`: it kills mutations (1) and (2) and is immune to the forward bleed round 1 found, because the offender has both a predecessor and a successor. Then strengthen line 106 to `assertThat(out).contains("12 verb(s) metered").contains("FaultInjectingStore.java")`, which kills (3) and (4) and makes the ok line a scope claim rather than a mood. If the exact 12 is felt to be brittle beside check-file-size's ceiling, assert the path and have the python print the number of verbs it examined so the grep-derived COUNT and the loop cannot disagree in silence -- today they are two independent mechanisms and nothing ties them together.

findings.finding: The refusal rows cannot tell 'refused for the right reason' from 'refused'. `not metered` and `first statement is` are both generic headline text that every unmetered-verb refusal prints -- unmetered, far-away, metered-on-one-branch-only and commented-out all emit BOTH strings, so the four rows' expected texts are interchangeable. Mutation that survives all six rows: replace `sig = next((s.strip() for s in src[i:i+3] if 'public' in s), line.strip())` with `sig = src[0].strip(); i = 0`, so every refusal blames line 1 and the SPDX header instead of the offending verb. A second surviving mutation: `print('\n'.join(missing[:1]))` -- if two verbs are unmetered only the first is ever named.
findings.failure_scenario: An author adds a verb, the hook refuses, and the message names the wrong line or the wrong verb -- in unmetered.java the offender is `presign` at :17 while `get` at :21 is fine, and nothing in the suite would notice the two being swapped. The gate's entire value on refusal is telling the author which verb to fix; a misdirecting message costs the author the search the gate was written to save, and with `missing[:1]` a split that unmeters several verbs at once is fixed one hook run at a time. Fails closed, so this is a minor.
findings.suggestion: The strings are already in the output: assert the verb and the line, e.g. an expectedText of `unmetered.java:17` / `presign` for the unmetered row and `:12` / `get` elsewhere. One more column in the CsvSource, or chain a second contains(...).

findings.finding: No fixture pins the one-line body, in either direction. `@Override public void close() { record("close"); }` is REFUSED by the gate today -- I ran it: the brace opens on the signature line, the rest of that line is skipped, and the 'first statement' reported is the NEXT verb's @Override line. That is a false refusal and it fails closed, so it is not a defect in itself; the exposure is that the obvious fix is unfalsifiable. Mutation that survives all six rows: `if '@Override' not in line or is_comment(line) or 'record(' in line: continue` -- a plausible-looking one-line-body fix that makes ANY @Override whose own line mentions record( exempt, including a commented-out one. (The tighter two-line variant, `'record(' not in ''.join(src[i:i+2])`, IS killed by commented-out.java, which is that fixture earning its keep.)
findings.failure_scenario: Someone writes `@Override public void close() { record("close"); }` after the split -- close() is the verb most likely to be a one-liner, and it is one of the three verbs M5.29's history names -- the hook refuses a correctly metered verb, and the fix is written as the exempt-the-signature-line version above. Every fixture stays green while the gate now skips any verb whose declaration line mentions record( at all.
findings.suggestion: Add the one-line metered body to metered.java as a third verb (green today only if the script handles it; it does not, so this is a red-first decision for the author: either accept the refusal and add it to an unmetered-shaped fixture documenting that the style is banned, or fix the script and pin the accepted shape).
